The way you are presenting it is circular, strictly speaking, but it is sufficient opening for my point:

We can not prove 2 + 2 = 4 unless we:

  1. Assign specific meanings of symbols involved (which you attempted above); and
  2. Define the rules for natural numbers (like Peano's Axioms) and for addition operation.

Since kindergarten, we get so familiar with one meaning of these symbols and one set of the rules applicable that we take them for granted. There are other meanings of say the '+' sign in use, but we ignore than unless the context warrants it. Thus, the mathematical statement 2 + 2 = 4 has a unique, unambiguous meaning in general discussion. We intuitively know what we are talking about when we talk about 'proving 2 + 2 = 4' even if we don't know the exact way to do it.

Can we deal with the concept of God in the same way? Do we have an intuitive understanding of the task when we talk about 'proving existence of God'? Obviously not.
But is it because God is subject of faith rather than knowledge/analysis? I think not.
I hold that there is no one familiar meaning or definition for God that can be taken for granted (unlike the case of 2 & 4 in 2 + 2 = 4). The meaning of the word God is not only ambiguous but also non-unique - two randomly selected Christians may easily have two different concepts of God.

So where does faith step in? I am not entirely sure of it. I think that when we talk about faith in God, we do it to simplify things. We do not need the ambiguity of our varied concepts of God. One concept, as we personally understand God, is sufficient for each of us. But we do need each other as a society or as a community. Faith helps us here, somehow.

Eberhard von Eisendorf, leader of the Spartacus League (SKB), wondered if maybe he’d made a monumental mistake today.

Now, granted, life so far had been pretty good. He has a nice apartment in Berlin, he was a member of the Bundestag, he had a pretty wife, and his office was nice. His hometown of Eisendorf over in Rendsburg-Eckernförde had trusted him so much they put him into the Bundestag, so he had plenty of friends to love back home. The plants he kept around livened things up, as did his obligatory bookshelf. There was even a fish tank that he enjoyed taking care of.

Across from his desk (a very spiffy desk), a handsome man sat in a chair. The tall man in the nice, custom-tailored suit had lovely blue eyes and hair so blonde it was almost white. His smile almost wiped away any feeling of anxiety that von Eisendorf had.

The problem was that this man was Gustav Steiner, leader of the DNVP, and a man blessed with the Devil’s own charisma.

And what was worth: when Steiner spoke, it sounded so reasonable, and it just made sense to von Eisendorf. That thought struck and icicle of fear into his heart.

“My point is,” Steiner went on, looking him straight in the eye, “when you get down to it, we are not so different in our values. You’re a nationalistic socialist of a sort. I am a national socialist. Why, yes, there are some finer differences here and there, but overall we see eye to eye on more things than not, hence why your party so often votes in favor of the bills I propose, whether they pass or not, and vice verse for us to you. The fact is, Herr von Eisendorf,” Steiner went on, leaning back an inch, “our party members get along very well. After all, you yourself joined the recent Tag der Deutschen Einheit rallies we held in Schleswig-Holstein. And many SKB members, like the former AfD, have marched with us on other such holidays, such as the Sedantag. All in all, we are very close parties, whether you like it or not.”

Von Eisendorf nodded. “I do admit, we are much friendlier than you would think we ought be. For a Nazi, you’re not so bad. But… you’re still a Nazi, and…” He rubbed the back of his head.

“What if I were to tell you that I wasn’t,” Steiner mentioned in offhanded tone, eying von Eisendorf’s aquarium. “Or at least that I won’t be one for much longer.”

“Come again?”

Steiner gave a grave nod. “I have been doing some thinking. I come to you to talk because despite us not being official allies, we work together more often than not.
